note.text: Useful money is generally acceptable, recognisable, durable, portable and divisible into workable units. These qualities help it perform functions but do not alone make every object money. Commodity money has a non-monetary commodity use; fiat currency does not depend on an equivalent commodity content. Banknotes and coins differ from transferable bank deposits. A card or cheque may instruct payment using a balance without being that balance itself. This is an economic distinction, not a guide to opening accounts or identifying counterfeits.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to compare useful qualities of money and distinguish cash, deposits and payment instruments. Builds on: money’s functions and barter. Leads to: money demand, supply and banking.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: A fictional market compares a bulky perishable crop with an accepted currency for small payments. Divisibility and durability can help explain the choice. In Cameroon the BEAC issues the common Central African CFA currency; deposit balances at commercial banks are a different form of monetary claim. A payment card accesses an account rather than storing every payment as physical notes.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Separate a quality from a function and a form from its payment instrument. Explain why a quality helps exchange without assuming that it guarantees acceptance everywhere. Ask which institution owes or issues the monetary claim.
